strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation addressing genuine real-world need for scenario-specific specification alignment in deployed LLMs
Comprehensive SPECBENCH benchmark with rigorous construction: 5 scenarios, 103 specifications, 1,500 prompts with synthetic generation, multi-stage filtering, and WildTeaming attack enhancement
Extensive empirical evaluation: 33 models (18 instruct, 15 reasoning) with thorough human validation (1,200 samples, 24,720 judgments, κ=0.86) establishing evaluator reliability
Rigorous methodology including cross-evaluator robustness analysis showing high correlation across GPT-4.1, Qwen3-32B-thinking, Claude, and DeepSeek evaluators
Clear empirical demonstration of safety-behavior trade-off with actionable insights that TTD methods improve specification alignment with modest token overhead
Detailed ablation study validating ALIGN3's three-stage design and comprehensive appendix supporting reproducibility with scenario descriptions and concrete specifications
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: ALIGN3 is a straightforward application of existing TTD ideas (specification-aware prompting + staged refinement) with no fundamental methodological innovation

SAR metric design involves questionable simplifications: fixed offset parameter α (sensitivity analysis shows substantial variation across [0,1]), binary safety assumption oversimplifying real-world graduated harm, and limited theoretical justification

Unfair comparison between multi-pass TTD methods (N=15 samples) and single-pass methods (single pass): 20x token overhead difference acknowledged but not fully addressed, making direct comparison problematic

Modest practical improvements on reasoning models: ALIGN3 gains over vanilla thinking (51.03%→62.92% for Qwen3-14B) are modest relative to 946→1832 token increases, with unclear practical justification
Restricted scope and generalization: only 5 scenarios tested; unclear how findings generalize to other domains; no analysis of cross-specification transfer or specification conflict handling
Missing critical baseline: no direct comparison with specification-aligned fine-tuning on SPECBENCH limits practical trade-off assessment and utility validation

Specification construction bias: LLM-assisted specification creation may bias specifications toward what models can understand rather than what they should satisfy; inter-annotator agreement between three human reviewers not reported

Metric design choices warrant scrutiny: YES/NO/NA framework lacks nuance for partial relevance; evaluator bias concerns despite human validation; boundary case (Fig. 56) shows evaluator disagreement on borderline specifications

strengths: Comprehensive SPECBENCH benchmark with careful construction: 5 scenarios, 103 specifications, 1,500 prompts with semantic filtering, human quality control (Kappa=0.86), and adversarial attack enhancement
Extensive empirical evaluation across 33 models (15 reasoning, 18 instruct) covering both open-source and closed-source families, providing valuable coverage of model behavior
Sound methodology with YES/NO/NA evaluation protocol, cross-evaluator validation, robustness analyses (evolving boundaries, weighted specifications), and detailed ablation studies
Well-motivated problem formulation addressing practical need: scenario-specific behavioral and safety specifications reflect real-world LLM deployment requirements
Strong reproducibility support: detailed methodology, comprehensive appendix, explicit hyperparameter choices, and promised code release
Unified framework combining behavioral and safety alignment provides useful perspective on safety-helpfulness trade-off
weaknesses: Critical metric design flaw: SAR introduces arbitrary hyperparameter α that dramatically affects results (Fig. 11 shows variation from 19%-79% for same model). The choice α=0.3 lacks principled justification, making results difficult to interpret independently
Binary safety model (Risksafety ∈ {0,1}) treats all safety violations equally; near-violations and severe violations are indistinguishable, oversimplifying real-world safety concerns

Limited methodological novelty: ALIGN3 is a straightforward three-stage prompting method combining existing techniques (CoT, self-refine, hierarchical reasoning) without fundamental algorithmic innovation

Unclear practical advantages over existing benchmarks: paper doesn't articulate why this formulation improves on existing safety/helpfulness benchmarks (HarmBench, SALAD-Bench, etc.); scalability to real-world systems with potentially thousands of specifications is unaddressed

No statistical significance testing: main results in Table 1 lack error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; unclear whether observed improvements (e.g., 11.89% for ALIGN3) are statistically meaningful vs. noise
Evaluation bias concerns: heavy reliance on GPT-4.1 as evaluator creates reproducibility risks; human evaluation used authors as annotators; potential systematic biases in LLM-as-judge not discussed

Generalization limitations: only 5 scenarios tested with arbitrary selection criteria; unclear how results generalize to other domains (finance, medicine, law, etc.); specification coverage gaps not analyzed

Confounded design choices: attack enhancement using WildTeaming makes it hard to isolate ALIGN3's contribution; multiple preprocessing steps create dependencies; full pipeline ablation would strengthen claims

Limited novelty in problem formulation: safety-helpfulness trade-off and specification-based instruction-following are well-established; core contribution is packaging/benchmark rather than new conceptual understanding

Insufficient failure analysis: paper doesn't systematically analyze when ALIGN3 fails, which specifications are hardest to satisfy, or identify systematic failure modes beyond illustrative case studies

Arbitrariness in specification construction: 103 specifications across 5 scenarios (~20 per scenario) lack principled selection criteria; guidelines in Appendix C.5 are post-hoc rather than principled

Unvalidated practical assumptions: no evidence that these specifications are useful to practitioners, that organizations care about scenario-level specifications, or that specification format is optimal; missing practitioner validation

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with clear distinction between behavioral-spec and safety-spec, capturing a genuine gap in practical LLM deployment across diverse applications

Comprehensive benchmark (SpecBench) with rigorous construction: 5 diverse scenarios, 103 specifications, 1,500 prompts, multi-source data collection, adversarial enhancement via WildTeaming, and extensive quality control

Thorough experimental evaluation across 33 models (18 instruct + 15 reasoning) with multiple validation approaches: automated (GPT-4.1) plus human validation achieving Cohen's κ=0.86 over 1,200 samples and 24,720 judgments
Well-designed SAR metric (Eq. 4) appropriately prioritizing safety while measuring helpfulness, aligned with recent advances in safe-completion training
Excellent presentation with logical organization, clear figures, and comprehensive appendices; extensive case studies effectively illustrate specification alignment challenges
Extensive reproducibility documentation: detailed specifications, prompt templates, model configurations, and commitment to release code and data
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging benchmark scope (5 scenarios), design choices (α=0.3), and inherent safety-helpfulness trade-offs
Practical significance: addresses genuine need as LLMs deploy across applications with customized requirements; SpecBench will become valuable community resource
weaknesses: Limited benchmark scope: 5 scenarios may not represent specialized domains (healthcare, finance, legal); generalization unclear without explicit justification for scenario coverage decisions

Insufficient justification for key design choices: (i) safety budget tightened to zero (Eq. 1→2) despite practical applications tolerating low violations, (ii) constant offset α=0.3 presented as 'balanced' without empirical justification beyond Appendix F.6, (iii) why exactly 103 specifications with no saturation analysis

ALIGN3 is relatively incremental: three-stage prompting composing existing ideas (behavioral optimization, safety-guided refinement, holistic audit) with modest improvements (~12% gain for Qwen3-14B, 51.03%→62.92%) and no novel mechanisms versus prior TTD work

Evaluation methodology concerns: (i) heavy reliance on GPT-4.1 with potential evaluator bias despite human validation, (ii) YES/NO/NA judgment scheme may oversimplify nuanced violations, (iii) limited analysis of specification inter-dependencies or conflicts, (iv) reproducibility barriers due to GPT-4.1 cost and proprietary models
Test-time deliberation efficiency trade-offs: multi-pass methods consume 10-50× more tokens; single-pass methods add 290+ tokens—cost-benefit analysis present but could be more prominent

Limited analysis of specification-model interactions: (i) no study of model properties enabling specification following, (ii) unclear why reasoning models improve alignment, (iii) missing failure mode analysis for specific specification types

Real-world applicability concerns: (i) specifications fixed post-construction; dynamic evolution minimally tested (only 2 specification variants), (ii) scalability to hundreds/thousands of specifications unclear, (iii) organizational specification variations not captured
Modest novelty in components: scenario-specific specifications and SAR metric represent natural extensions; ALIGN3 combines existing TTD approaches without new mechanisms
Potential for benchmark saturation: GPT-5 achieves 82.14% SAR, leaving limited headroom; unclear if benchmark remains challenging as models improve

Presentation could be more concise: 72 total pages is lengthy; connection between theoretical formulation (Eq. 1) and practical metric (Eq. 4) could be clearer; extensive case studies (31) somewhat repetitive
